summary: First English narrative draft for tetraethyl-lead-1924: the late-1924 choice between pressing to resume the patented anti-knock additive and dropping it for ethanol blends, with decision quality argued from what was visible at T0 rather than from the half-century that followed.

narrative.hook: It is November 1924. The men who make your fuel additive are dead -- at three plants now, not one. The state has locked the Bayway works, some cities have banned the fuel outright, and Washington is convening to decide whether any of it should ever restart.
narrative.short_setup: Three years earlier, General Motors researchers found that a small amount of tetraethyl lead in gasoline all but eliminated engine knock, the limit on how hard an engine could be pushed. GM patented it, formed the Ethyl Corporation with Standard Oil of New Jersey, and had DuPont manufacture it. Then the men making the concentrate began to die -- first at DuPont's Deepwater plant from September 1923, then at GM's Dayton pilot plant, and finally, between late September and October 1924, at Standard Oil's Bayway refinery in Linden, New Jersey, where workers suffered hallucinations and violent mania before several of them died and dozens more were hospitalised. New Jersey shut the unit down. The companies must now decide what to argue for, and the Surgeon General must decide what to allow. There is an alternative: ethanol blends, which GM's own engineers had already tested and found to work. It has one commercial defect. Nobody can own it.
narrative.why_option_a_made_sense: The argument for resuming rested on a distinction that was standard industrial reasoning in 1924: a substance dangerous to manufacture is not necessarily dangerous to use. The deaths happened where the concentrate was handled at full strength, by a small number of workers, in a process that could be engineered against -- better ventilation, enclosed transfer, protective equipment, rotation off the unit. In finished gasoline the additive was present at a tiny fraction, and burned. Against that, the claim that lead dispersed in exhaust would slowly accumulate in millions of ordinary people was, at that moment, an argument from what lead was known to do at industrial doses, extended to a scale nobody could measure. No instrument existed that could confirm or refute it. And tetraethyl lead genuinely worked better than anything else available: the engineering problem it solved was real, and solving it had real value to a country rapidly putting itself on wheels.
narrative.why_option_b_made_sense: The case for stopping did not require winning the argument about exhaust at all. It rested on two things already in hand. First, the additive had killed people at three separate plants over more than a year. That was not a hypothesis about the future; it was a record. The industry's own answer -- that better handling would fix it -- had been available before Bayway too, and Bayway still happened. Second, a substitute existed and had already been tested inside General Motors. Ethanol blends suppressed knock without the same acute toxicity. Choosing them meant accepting a worse anti-knock margin, a larger blend fraction, real complications under Prohibition -- and the surrender of a patent position that every competitor would then share. Those were substantial costs. They were also, entirely, commercial costs, weighed against a hazard that had already been proven in the only way hazards are proven.
narrative.actual_decision_explanation: The companies pressed to resume, and won. Production stayed voluntarily suspended through the Public Health Service conference of 20 May 1925 in Washington, where Standard Oil's Frank Howard defended the additive as an important industrial advance and argued that its dilution in finished gasoline made ordinary use safe, while Yandell Henderson and the industrial toxicologist Alice Hamilton pressed the case for population-level risk and further study. The Surgeon General appointed an investigative committee. In January 1926 it reported that it found no good grounds for prohibiting the sale of leaded gasoline when properly diluted and handled, while recommending continued study and stronger protection for production workers. Sale resumed.
narrative.outcome_story: Leaded petrol became the American standard and stayed there for roughly fifty years. The recommended further study was never seriously funded. The tools that could have settled the 1924 argument did not exist until the geochemist Clair Patterson built them: working from the late 1950s on contamination-free measurement, he showed in 1965 that industrial lead, chiefly from gasoline exhaust, accounted for the overwhelming majority of lead found in the environment and in human bodies, far above any natural background. That finding fed into the 1970 Clean Air Act, unleaded fuel for new American cars from 1975, and a complete U.S. ban for on-road vehicles in 1996. A large body of later epidemiology links population-wide lead exposure, especially in childhood, to measurable neurological and cognitive harm.
narrative.hindsight_analysis: This case is easy to score badly, because almost everyone now knows how it ends. Knowing the ending makes the 1924 choice look obvious, and it was not obvious in the way we imagine -- but the decision still comes out weak, and for reasons that were visible at the time rather than in 1965. Start with what the resumption argument got right. The occupational-versus-use distinction was not invented for this controversy; it was how the era thought about industrial chemistry generally, and it is not simply wrong. The dilution really was small. The exhaust hypothesis really was unmeasurable, and would stay unmeasurable for four decades. In 1924 there was no regulatory category for diffuse, slow, population-scale harm from a product safe to touch, and the burden of proof sat, as a matter of convention, on whoever claimed the harm. A company asked to abandon its patent on an unprovable hypothesis had a genuine answer. Now the part that does not survive. The case for stopping never depended on that hypothesis. Men were already dead, at three plants, over more than a year, and the substitute was already tested and sitting inside the company that chose against it. Strip out the exhaust argument entirely and the decision is still: keep making the thing that kills the people who make it, because the safe version cannot be patented. Two further things were plainly visible in November 1924 without any hindsight. The people warning about population exposure -- Henderson, Hamilton -- had credentials and no commercial stake, and were discounted by parties who had a very large one. And the federal review convened to settle the question had no independent testing capacity, which everyone involved could see; it was going to be answered substantially with data supplied by the industry whose product was on trial. A process that cannot check the interested party's numbers is not much of a check, and that was knowable before it reported. Score the outcome separately, and carefully. It was bad -- half a century of exposure, and a body of evidence linking it to real harm in children. But the causal line runs through many later decisions too, and the counterfactual is not free: whether Prohibition-era America could actually have supplied ethanol at national scale is a genuinely open question, and switching in 1924 would have traded a known disaster for an unknown one. What makes this weak is not that they guessed wrong about the future. It is that they were not really guessing about the present, and preferred the answer that kept the patent.
narrative.decision_principle: When a hazard is already proven and a workable substitute is already in hand, the burden of proof has moved: continuing is the claim that needs defending, not stopping. And a review that cannot independently check the interested party's evidence is not a finding of safety -- it is the absence of one.
narrative.longform_story:
In December 1921, in a laboratory in Dayton, Ohio, Thomas Midgley Jr. found that adding a small quantity of tetraethyl lead to gasoline all but eliminated knock -- the premature detonation that had put a hard ceiling on how much compression an engine could take, and therefore on power and fuel economy. It was a real solution to a real problem, arrived at after a long and unglamorous search through a great many compounds. General Motors patented it. GM and Standard Oil of New Jersey formed the Ethyl Corporation to sell it, and DuPont made it.

Midgley and his colleagues had also tested ethanol blends, which suppressed knock too. Ethanol needed a much larger fraction to do the same work, and it had one insurmountable commercial problem: anybody with a still could make it. There was no patent to be had, no licence to charge, no position to hold. Tetraethyl lead offered all three. That asymmetry was not a secret and not a discovery of later historians; it was the ordinary business logic of the venture, plain to everyone inside it.

The trouble began where the concentrate was made. At DuPont's Deepwater plant in New Jersey, workers began dying in September 1923. There were deaths at GM's Dayton pilot plant too. Then, between roughly 26 September and 30 October 1924, the tetraethyl lead unit at Standard Oil's Bayway refinery in Linden, New Jersey produced a run of casualties severe enough to reach the front pages: men hallucinating, some violently manic, several dead -- detailed chronologies name six, some summaries five -- with dozens more hospitalised and some requiring long-term institutional care. Standard Oil's first public explanation was that the men had been overworked. Outside physicians and health officials disputed that immediately.

New Jersey shut the unit down and barred a restart without state permission. Some cities banned the sale of the fuel. Production stopped, and the Surgeon General began organising a federal review. This is the decision point: not whether to invent leaded gasoline, which was already invented and already selling, but whether to fight for its return.

The argument the companies brought was coherent. Making tetraethyl lead was dangerous; using it was a different question. Concentrate handling could be engineered -- ventilation, enclosure, protective gear, limits on exposure time. In the tank of a car the additive was present in a very small proportion and then burned. The warning that mattered most for the public came from Yale's Yandell Henderson, who argued that lead dispersed from millions of exhaust pipes would accumulate slowly in the general population, a different danger from the acute poisoning of the men on the unit. It was a serious argument from a serious scientist. It was also, in 1924, unmeasurable. Nobody had an instrument clean enough to distinguish industrial lead from natural background in a human body or in the air.

On 20 May 1925 the Public Health Service convened a conference in Washington. Standard Oil's Frank Howard defended the additive as an important industrial advance and rested on the dilution argument. Henderson pressed the exposure case. Alice Hamilton, who had spent her career documenting what industry did to the people inside it, urged caution and further study. The Surgeon General appointed an investigative committee.

The committee reported in January 1926. It found no good grounds for prohibiting the sale of leaded gasoline when properly diluted and handled. It recommended continued study, and better protection for the men making it. Sale resumed almost at once. The continued study was not seriously resourced, and no comparable federal reconsideration followed for forty-four years.

What the committee could not do was test anything at scale independently. It had neither the money nor the apparatus, and much of what it worked from came from the industry whose product it was reviewing. Historians -- Gerald Markowitz and David Rosner most prominently -- have read this as a process substantively shaped by that industry. Contemporaneous Public Health Service framing reads it as an honest inquiry hobbled by its own thinness. The records do not settle how much was influence and how much was incapacity, and this account does not pretend to settle it either. What can be said without taking a side is that a review unable to check the interested party's numbers could not have produced a finding of safety worth much, and that limitation was visible in 1925, not only in retrospect.

For the next half-century, American cars burned lead. The question the 1925 conference could not answer was finally answered by someone who had not been looking for it. Clair Patterson, a geochemist trying to date the Earth, found that his samples were being ruined by lead contamination from the modern world, and spent years building measurement clean enough to work at all. By 1965 he could show that the lead in the environment, and in people, was overwhelmingly industrial in origin, chiefly from gasoline, and vastly above any natural baseline. That work fed the 1970 Clean Air Act, unleaded fuel for new cars from 1975, and a full ban for American on-road vehicles in 1996. Decades of epidemiology since have tied population-level lead exposure, especially in childhood, to measurable neurological and cognitive damage.

So the outcome was bad. But the interesting judgement is the other one, and the two have to be kept apart. The men deciding in 1924 were not stupid, and they did not have Patterson. Their central factual claim -- that nobody could demonstrate harm from the diluted product in use -- was true, and stayed true for forty years. In a world without a category for slow, diffuse, population-scale harm, and with the burden of proof sitting on the accuser, that was a real defence.

The reason it still fails is that the case for stopping never needed the exhaust argument. The deaths at three plants were not a prediction. The substitute was not speculative; it had been tested in-house by the same company. Remove Henderson's warning from the record entirely and the decision reads the same way: continue making a substance that has killed its own workers, because the version that does not kill them cannot be owned. The warnings that were offered came from people with expertise and nothing to gain, and were weighed by people with a great deal to lose. The body convened to settle it could not independently check a single number it was given. None of that required hindsight.

It is worth resisting one last temptation, which is to assume the other road was clean. Supplying ethanol at national scale in Prohibition-era America was a genuinely uncertain proposition, and a 1924 switch would have traded a known hazard for an unmapped one. The failure here is not that they picked the wrong future. It is that they treated a settled present -- dead workers, a tested alternative, an evaluator who could not evaluate -- as though it were still an open question, and landed on the answer that kept the patent.
